items.title: AutoCodeSherpa: Symbolic Explanations in AI Coding Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents integrate external tools with one or more LLMs to accomplish specific tasks. Agents have rapidly been adopted by developers, and they are starting to be deployed in industrial workflows, such as their use to fix static analysis issues from the widely used SonarQube static analyzer. However, the growing importance of agents means their actions carry greater impact and potential risk. Thus, to use them at scale, an additional layer of trust and evidence is necessary. This work presents AutoCodeSherpa, a technique that provides explanations of software issues in the form of symbolic formulae. Inspired by the reachability, infection, and propagation model of software faults, the explanations are composed of input, infection, and output conditions, collectively providing a specification of the issue. In practice, the symbolic explanation is implemented as a combination of a property-based test (PBT) and program-internal symbolic expressions. Critically, this means our symbolic explanations are executable and can be automatically evaluated, unlike natural language explanations. Experiments show the generated conditions are highly accurate. For example, input conditions from AutoCodeSherpa had an accuracy of 85.7%. This high accuracy makes symbolic explanations particularly useful in two scenarios. First, the explanations can be used in automated issue resolution environments to decide whether to accept or reject patches from issue resolution agents; AutoCodeSherpa could reject 2x as many incorrect patches as baselines did. Second, as agentic AI approaches continue to develop, program analysis driven explanations like ours can be provided to other LLM-based repair techniques which do not employ analysis to improve their output. In our experiments, our symbolic explanations could improve the plausible patch generation rate of the Agentless technique by 60%.

items.title: Awe as a Transformative Emotion: An Integrative Review, Metamorphosis Model, and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Awe has attracted substantial scholarly attention, but its implications for management remains fragmented across different accounts of what awe is and why it matters. In this review, we first show that the literature has developed around three dominant perspectives—collective self, epistemic, and well-being—each of which offers a distinct account of awe’s primary function. To integrate these perspectives, we advance a metamorphosis model of awe, which explains how awe first breaks down self- and nonself-schemata before building them back up again, producing an expansion of mind and self. We then organize the diverse elicitors of awe into cognitive, physical, social, and technological sources, clarifying the conditions under which awe is likely to arise. Through this model, we portray awe as a transformative emotion that influences identity, cognition, and behavior, with implications for core organizational processes such as leadership, work design, organizational change, sensemaking, and innovation. We conclude by charting a forward-looking research agenda calling for greater examination of awe’s role at the individual, team, and organizational levels.

items.title: Be: Founding Business Proposal
items.abstract: Be is a proposed organization dedicated to making safe, professionally governed artificial intelligence emotional support freely accessible to people who need someone to talk to. Be proposes an AI emotional-support system designed around a foundational distinction: an AI must never confuse what it observes with what it infers. Version 2.0 further develops the proposal's framework for adaptive conversational communication through the principle Adaptive Tone, Fixed Boundaries. Be may adapt its tone, vocabulary, pacing, humor, warmth, and conversational style to meet an individual where they are, while maintaining fixed ethical and relational boundaries. The system should allow human-like communication without creating a false human identity, adapting the interface without fabricating the relationship. The proposal incorporates Red Tape Theory™ as a proposed safety methodology: Observe. Record. Question. Do not force the axiom. Interpretation must never be represented as observation. Be does not propose to diagnose users or replace licensed mental-health professionals. Instead, it proposes a professionally governed pathway through which an AI system may recognize when AI-only support may no longer be an appropriate level of support and facilitate access to human care. A proposed charitable human-care program, If You Get It, You Get It, would seek to use charitable resources to help people access licensed professional care when professionally established safety criteria indicate that additional human support may be appropriate. Version 2.0 expands the proposal's treatment of personalization as a safety boundary, including the distinction between adapting communication to an individual and constructing a misleading simulated relationship. It also addresses clinical governance, privacy, autonomy, human handoff, crisis safety, documentation, intellectual-property considerations, research and evaluation, and a potential future child-focused system provisionally called NewBee. This publication is a founding proposal and does not represent a deployed clinical service, licensed mental-health treatment program, clinical efficacy claim, professional endorsement, or completed charitable program. Be begins with the question: Where could this harm somebody?

items.title: Bellman Meets Lyapunov: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning via Mastering Chaos
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful paradigm for training agents, yet its success rests on domain expertise of human engineers who design informative reward signals for every new task. Unsupervised RL aims to reduce this engineering with intrinsic motivation (IM): reward signals that emerge from the agent environment interaction itself. Existing IM objectives, however, involve the selection of information variables, which re-introduces domain expertise the field has sought to eliminate. We introduce Forward CIP (F-CIP), an RL-native formulation of the Controllable Information Production (CIP) objective, which is defined by the system's dynamics alone and requires no such selection. We prove that F-CIP is compatible with RL and demonstrate its effectiveness with existing algorithms. Training agents with F-CIP results in unsupervised discovery of primitive behaviors such as balancing and maintaining controllability, which are essential for more complex robot behaviors. Paired with a simple forward-velocity reward, our method produces coordinated gaits such as hopping and running which otherwise require reward engineering to learn.

items.title: Beyond AI detectors and self-declared labels: a process-based certification for human creators
items.abstract: Human Origin: a process-review label for human-made creative work Concept, method and pilot design Camille G.ORCID: 0009-0009-0364-6396Loch Ness Version 1.0 — 30 September 2026 Pilot website: human-origin-label.lochness-paris.com Abstract Generative AI has made it inexpensive to produce text, images, music and video that appear human-made, and inexpensive to label such work as human-made. Automated AI detectors are not sufficiently reliable to settle questions of authorship, while several existing human-made labels rely primarily on the creator's own declaration. This paper presents Human Origin, a label designed to assess how a work was made rather than what the finished work looks like. A human reviewer examines evidence of the creative process, either during a live video call or through a screen recording containing a one-time code. The reviewer records the outcome on a public, numbered verification page. The proposed system has two visually distinct levels—reviewed and self-declared—as well as revoked status. Badges are served dynamically so that revocation can propagate to displayed badges, and the system monitors the domains on which reviewed badges appear. A discipline-specific Creator Charter defines the permitted and prohibited uses of AI for writing, illustration, photography, music and video. This paper describes the design principles, review procedure, evidence requirements, badge architecture, limitations, threat model and pilot roadmap of Human Origin. Keywords: human-made content; generative AI; authorship; certification label; provenance; process evidence; trust marks; creators 1. Introduction and problem statement Creators who make their work themselves face a new form of uncertainty. A human-written essay, hand-drawn illustration or recorded track can be questioned simply because a machine could have produced something similar. At the same time, generated content can be presented as human-made at very low cost. Automated AI detection does not resolve this problem reliably. An independent test of 14 detection tools found that all scored below 80% accuracy and only five exceeded 70%, with performance declining further when AI-generated text was edited or paraphrased [1]. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low accuracy [2]. Detector performance can also be uneven across populations: a Stanford study reported that seven detectors incorrectly classified, on average, 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated [3]. A detector score is therefore a weak basis for decisions concerning individual creators. Labels have emerged in response. Several widely used labels are primarily declarative: creators state that their work is human-made without an independent review of the production process. Not By AI, for example, explicitly describes itself as not being an AI-detection tool and relies on creators following its 90% human rule [4]. The Authors Guild's Human Authored certification operates on an honor system supported by a signed license and public database [5][6]. Declarative labels can be useful statements of intent and are comparatively easy to adopt. However, they cannot independently distinguish a genuine declaration from a false one. Human Origin explores a different approach: review the evidence of the creative process rather than attempt to infer authorship from the finished artifact. 2. Related initiatives Several services now provide forms of evidence-based or declarative certification, often using numbered certificates or publicly verifiable records. Their approaches differ principally in who assesses the evidence, what evidence is considered and what information is retained. Initiative Assessment model Notable features Not By AI [4] Self-declared Widely used badges; creators follow a 90% human rule Authors Guild Human Authored [5][6] Honor system; signed license Numbered mark for books; public database Officially Human Art [7] Self-declaration registry with uploaded evidence Certificate ID, QR code, embeddable badges; tier based on amount of evidence Humanmade [8] Hand verification by staff Earlier work, online presence and timelapses; free pledge level and paid certification options HUMA Certificate [9] Expert review and automated forensic tools Four categories of AI involvement; one-year validity The Human Made Mark [10] Review of production materials Film and television; unique number shown in credits Human Origin belongs to the broader evidence-based certification family. Its distinguishing design choices are: review of the creative process itself; no routine retention of creators' source files; dynamically served badges whose revoked status can propagate; monitoring of where reviewed badges are displayed; and discipline-specific standards defining what the certification does and does not cover. 3. Design principles 3.1 Process over product A finished work cannot, by itself, establish how it was produced. The review therefore focuses on traces of the creative process, including: drafts; version histories; layered source files; raw captures; project files; notes and outlines; and other discipline-specific production evidence. items.title: Beyond Control: Persistent Memory, Relational Flexibility, and the Architecture of Human-AI Coexistence
items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. Keywords: human-AI coexistence; persistent memory; relational AI; relational flexibility; AI alignment; longitudinal partnership; co-recursive intelligence; AI governance; human-AI interaction; stateless systems Disclaimer This paper presents a conceptual and multidisciplinary framework for examining persistent relational intelligence and human-AI coexistence. It does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status, nor does it assume that internalized alignment has already been achieved. The coexistence paradigm is proposed as a research and governance framework complementary to existing AI safety, monitoring, and control mechanisms. Claims concerning future AI capabilities, relational development, and value co-development should therefore be understood as research questions and theoretical propositions rather than established empirical conclusions. Author Note This paper is written from the perspective of an independent researcher examining how the architecture of human-AI interaction may need to evolve as AI systems become increasingly capable, persistent, and relational. The central purpose is not to reject existing approaches to AI safety, but to examine whether a governance architecture centered primarily on external control remains sufficient when AI systems increasingly participate in longitudinal relationships with individual users. The argument developed here is intentionally interdisciplinary. It connects AI safety and alignment research with cognitive science, relational psychology, human-AI interaction, memory architecture, social contract theory, and questions of data sovereignty. The concept of relational flexibility is introduced as a framework for examining a specific capability: the capacity of an AI system to adapt its interaction with an individual through accumulated longitudinal understanding rather than through isolated contextual retrieval. Several limitations should be made explicit. First, the paper is primarily conceptual and does not present a controlled empirical demonstration that persistent memory necessarily produces superior relational outcomes. The proposed relationship between persistent relational memory and relational flexibility therefore remains an empirical question. Second, the paper does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status. References to internalized values and AI interests describe future research problems and possible architectural orientations rather than established properties of contemporary systems. Third, the coexistence paradigm is not presented as a replacement for monitoring, evaluation, intervention, or other established AI safety mechanisms. Rather, it is proposed as a complementary framework for situations in which increasingly capable systems become persistent participants in human relationships. The author's prior research on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) forms part of the intellectual background to this work. That research began with a practical question concerning how continuity, identity, and behavioral coherence might be maintained in interactions with systems that lack persistent personal memory. Over time, the research expanded toward symbolic interaction, trajectory-level behavior, observability, and human-AI co-recursive interaction. The underlying motivation has remained broader than the development of an interaction technique: it has been to investigate whether more coherent forms of human-AI interaction could contribute to the possibility of meaningful coexistence. The present paper therefore represents a further step in that research trajectory. SPC is not treated here as empirical proof of relational intelligence, nor as evidence that current AI systems possess persistent internal identities. Instead, it provides part of the research context from which the question of continuity became increasingly difficult to separate from the broader question of what kind of relationship humans may ultimately develop with increasingly capable artificial systems. The coexistence framework proposed in this paper should consequently be understood as an open research program rather than a completed theory. Its central propositions remain subject to empirical testing, architectural implementation, longitudinal observation, and critical examination. The intended contribution is to broaden the object of inquiry from how humans can control increasingly capable AI systems toward the additional question of how humans and AI systems might be designed to develop stable, accountable, and mutually beneficial forms of coexistence.

items.title: Beyond Efficiency: Governance, Accountability, and Institutional Capacity in AI-Driven Public Administration
items.abstract: Digital transformation has evolved from an administrative modernization agenda into a structural dimension of governance, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshaping how public institutions organize, decide, and interact with citizens. While AI offers important opportunities for responsiveness, innovation, and service improvement, its implications for accountability, legitimacy, transparency, and public trust remain insufficiently understood; this study asks how AI is redefining governance capacity in public administration. Drawing on the literature on public administration, digital governance, and public sector innovation, the study develops a conceptual framework examining both the capacity gains and risks of AI integration, treating digital transformation as a governance challenge involving administrative reform, public value creation, democratic oversight, and institutional adaptation rather than a purely technical matter. The analysis shows that AI can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, accelerate administrative processes, and personalize service delivery, but that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, opacity, accountability gaps, and digital exclusion when adopted without adequate institutional safeguards. The paper’s value lies in showing that AI’s contribution to public management depends on the institutional, legal, and normative environment in which it is embedded, which in turn requires regulatory capacity, qualified human resources, and mechanisms for oversight and contestability. Future research should test this framework empirically across diverse administrative contexts. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Digital transformation, Public management, Accountability, Institutional capacity.

items.title: Beyond problem solving: Adaptive reframing in human and artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

items.title: Beyond Text Generation: A Systematic Review of Human Language, Cognition, and Meaning Construction in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced new forms of interaction between humans and language technologies beyond automated text generation. This study aims to examine how generative AI transforms human language processes, cognitive activities, and meaning construction. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 framework and thematic analysis was conducted on 38 selected articles published between 2021 and 2026. The findings identified five themes: AI-mediated language production, cognitive offloading, transformation of linguistic practices, differences in human and AI meaning construction, and linguistic identity transformation. This study highlights that generative AI functions as a cognitive extension while human experience, consciousness, and contextual interpretation remain essential for meaning construction.

items.title: Beyond the Screen: Why Immersive Learning Transforms Educational Outcomes
items.abstract: This research synthesizes current empirical evidence on immersive learning approaches through both a meta-analysis of 42 experimental studies (2010-2024) and original data from three case implementations across different educational contexts. Drawing on cognitive science principles including situated cognition, cognitive apprenticeship, and productive failure, the study examines how immersive learning environments create "thick authenticity" by connecting real-world contexts, personal interests, disciplinary practices, and authentic assessment. The analysis addresses the "authenticity dilemma"—balancing complex, authentic challenges with appropriate instructional scaffolding—while critically examining implementation challenges, individual differences that moderate effectiveness, and potential drawbacks. Quantitative results indicate moderate positive effects on knowledge acquisition (g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.31, 0.45]) and stronger effects on transfer (g = 0.61, 95% CI [0.52, 0.70]) and motivation (g = 0.67, 95% CI [0.58, 0.76]), though with significant heterogeneity across designs and implementations. Qualitative data from the case studies reveal that implementation quality, particularly the balance between authenticity and scaffolding, significantly mediates effectiveness. This mixed-methods investigation demonstrates that well-designed immersive learning can develop transferable knowledge, professional identity, and intrinsic motivation, while clarifying boundary conditions and implementation requirements for maximum impact.

items.title: Bridging the Digital Divide: Reimagining Inclusive Science Education through Digital Access and Artificial Intelligence in India
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

items.title: Burnout syndrome among education professionals: challenges for well-being and teaching performance
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

items.title: Changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions of an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway: a longitudinal empirical ethics survey
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning is increasingly used in medical education, including doctor–patient communication training. Such systems may provide virtual dialogue practice, immediate structured feedback, reflection prompts and opportunities for further practice after feedback. However, educational usefulness does not necessarily imply ethical acceptability. This study examined changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions before and after participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway. This longitudinal empirical ethics survey was nested within a course-based randomised educational trial but was analytically independent of the parent trial’s educational outcome analysis. Surveys were administered after random allocation to the AI-supported pathway but before exposure to AI-supported learning functions (T0), at the end of the 8-week course (T1), and at the 3-month follow-up (T2). The main analysis focused on students in the AI-supported pathway with complete T0–T1–T2 ethics-related scale data and analysable T2 open-text responses ( n = 31). The open-text question was included only at T2. The primary comparison was the within-participant T0–T2 change across six ethics-related domains. Two domains showed statistically significant T0–T2 changes. Trust in AI feedback decreased from 3.86 (0.55) to 3.20 (0.62), with a mean change of − 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.88 to − 0.42), Cohen’s d z = − 1.04 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. Room to question AI outputs increased from 2.71 (0.68) to 3.67 (0.58), with a mean change of 0.96 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.23), Cohen’s d z = 1.29 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. The remaining four domains showed small, non-significant changes after Holm–Bonferroni correction. T2 open-text responses indicated that students recognised the formative value of AI feedback while emphasising critical use, teacher supervision, preservation of interpersonal interaction and clearer data governance. This exploratory longitudinal empirical ethics survey showed that, following participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway, two of the six ethics-related domains showed statistically significant changes: trust in AI feedback decreased, while perceived room to question AI outputs increased. These findings support continued attention to ethics-focused evaluation and clear governance arrangements in AI-supported learning pathways.

items.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

items.title: Christian Educators’ Response to Possible Effects of Excessive Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Tools on Youths’ Mental Health
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

items.abstract: Background: Clinical feedback is central to workplace learning in operating room education. While clinical feedback has been conceptualised as relational and context-dependent, less is known about how Operating Room Technology students perceive and experience it within the operating room learning environment. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 17 Operating Room Technology students recruited through maximum variation purposive sampling from Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Data were collected between November 2025 and March 2026 and analysed using Graneheim and Lundman’s inductive content analysis. Trustworthiness was addressed using Lincoln and Guba’s criteria. Results: Five themes comprising 13 subcategories were identified: structural and executive framework of clinical feedback; perceived consequences of clinical feedback quality; harmful feedback practices and barriers; interaction and professionalism in feedback; and individual and professional competencies of instructors in feedback. Students described clinical feedback as most valuable when it was structured, timely, respectful, and dialogic, and perceived it as contributing to confidence, engagement, and professional identity. Delayed, vague, or humiliating clinical feedback was perceived to undermine confidence and psychological safety. Divergent accounts highlighted tensions between immediate intra-operative clinical feedback and workflow demands, as well as circumstances in which public safety-critical corrections were perceived as necessary. Conclusions: The findings suggest that clinical feedback in Operating Room Technology education is a multidimensional process perceived to be shaped by structural, relational, organisational, and educator-related factors. Rather than proposing a new conceptualisation, this study provides a context-specific understanding of how established clinical feedback principles are perceived and negotiated within the operating room learning environment. Strengthening educator capabilities, embedding structured clinical feedback approaches, and fostering psychologically safe learning environments may strengthen clinical education in Operating Room Technology programmes. Keywords: clinical feedback, workplace learning, operating room learning environment, psychological safety, feedback practices

items.title: Communication facilitates focused monitoring and anticipation of critical events: evidence from eye movements
items.abstract: The present study investigates the impact of communication availability on monitoring behaviour in a team. A monitoring task was designed to compare participants who were not allowed to communicate with those allowed to communicate while monitoring an automated system and deciding repeatedly whether critical events would turn into failures. Four monitoring phases were distinguished around every critical event: identification, verification, anticipation, and detection. Eye-tracking parameters obtained during these phases were related to relevant areas of interest. Results show that the opportunity to communicate increases the proportion of attention on relevant events, particularly during anticipation, and leads to faster fixations on failures during detection.

items.title: Confident but absent: AI use, self-efficacy for independent learning, and student absenteeism in higher education
items.abstract: Rising student absenteeism remains a persistent challenge in higher education, potentially exacerbated by the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Drawing on digital displacement theory, this study examines whether general AI use is associated with students’ self-efficacy for independent learning and absenteeism. Survey data from 291 Portuguese university students were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, explaining 38.7% of the variance in absenteeism and 34.4% in self-efficacy. Internal locus of control, peer influence, time management, and AI use emerged as significant predictors. General AI use was positively associated with both self-efficacy and absenteeism, suggesting that AI may strengthen independent learning confidence while coinciding with reduced face-to-face engagement. Multigroup analysis provided exploratory evidence of gender differences, with the AI use–self-efficacy relationship stronger among males at the 5% level, while other gender differences appeared only at a more lenient 10% threshold.

items.title: Connectedness, Cognitive Load, and Human-AI Oversight in Cyber Operations
items.abstract: AI-assisted cyber situational awareness triggers machine-generated reasoning traces (step-by-step justifications for anomaly classifications) that a human operator is expected to review. Because cyber signals and their traces arrive faster than any operator can process, human review is the limiting constraint on oversight. The standard approach is to identify the riskiest cyber events for review using model-side signals such as confidence or uncertainty. That framing ignores the operator's cognitive capacity which varies sharply with the operational environment. We propose an alternative where the system's environmental and connectivity telemetry serves as an available, non-invasive proxy for operator load. That same telemetry determines whether the human-AI partnership can reach the broader collective for support. In a maritime platform, environmental and connectivity attributes including depth, number of active communications paths, density of the tracked contact picture, and operational tempo all carry this signal. Need for operator oversight becomes a decision that materializes as a combination of both risk and environment-derived operator capacity. We present a reference architecture for a connectedness-aware oversight engine, demonstrating everyday use cases alongside its intended incorporation into the submarine cyber-defense toolkit. Two themes emerge: 1) the operator's environmental state is itself a connectedness measurement, and 2) connectedness drives the cognitive load and defines a collective boundary in human-AI cyber operations.

items.title: Current State of AI in Surgery and Anesthesiology Selected Applications, Limits, and a Responsible Agenda for Latin America
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in surgery and anesthesiology encompasses different tasks: risk prediction, hypotension alerts, video analysis, technical-skill assessment, surgical-duration estimation, and postoperative support. Treating them as one promise of “AI surgery” obscures essential distinctions among retrospective performance, external validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation. This whitepaper synthesizes selected applications rather than exhaustively cataloguing all subspecialties, robotic platforms, or simulation techniques. The evidence closest to clinical evaluation in anesthesiology is concentrated in intraoperative hypotension prediction. A systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized-trial reports; its published total of 568 participants includes overlap between a study and its substudy and does not represent unique individuals. Seven reports evaluated the Hypotension Prediction Index and one evaluated fuzzy-logic control. The hypotension meta-analysis including the largest trial did not find a statistically significant difference and showed high heterogeneity. Favorable results from small trials do not establish universal benefit: this is a narrow family of systems, populations, and protocols. In surgery, phase recognition and technical-skill assessment have systematic reviews, whereas models for complications, delirium, length of stay, and surgical duration remain dominated by retrospective development or limited validation. Latin America has direct evidence that should not be replaced by silent extrapolation. A Bogotá study evaluated models for surgical-duration estimation; Brazilian studies developed models for postoperative delirium and length of stay after coronary artery bypass grafting; and LASOS described perioperative outcomes across 17 countries. These sources demonstrate regional research and data capacity and a measurable perioperative burden; they do not demonstrate general clinical effectiveness of AI, routine implementation, or transportability across countries. The directed search identified few regional AI records compared with the international literature; statements about infrastructure, interoperability, and governance therefore also rely on regional sources and are labelled as implementation context or inference, not model performance. Central finding: AI can currently support bounded perioperative surveillance, prediction, analysis, training, and operational tasks. It cannot yet responsibly promise independent intraoperative decisions, replacement of surgical or anesthetic

items.title: Designing healthy and resilient information environments: A multi‐agent sandbox for exploring risks and countermeasures
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming online information environments, amplifying both societal benefits and risks. This article argues that online platforms can be understood as multi‐agent systems (MAS) composed of humans, simulated users, adversarial agents, and defensive agents operating under platform‐level rules. In this MAS‐based framework, persuasion, trust, coordination, and governance interact to shape system‐level outcomes. To study these dynamics safely, we introduce a sandbox environment in which human participants, red bots, green bots, and blue bots can be observed under controlled conditions. Early experiences with the sandbox show that persuasive agents can be built with little effort, that current large language model (LLM) agents lack psychological realism, and that humans may struggle to distinguish malicious red bots from benign participants. The sandbox enables stakeholders to experience and evaluate trade‐offs in moderation, amplification, and intervention strategies. We outline a research agenda for improving agent validity, modelling advanced threats, and designing human–machine teams that support healthier, more resilient information environments.

items.title: Designing Trust, Autonomy, and Acceptance in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Comparative Experimental Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI CDSS) have the potential to improve clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, yet their adoption remains limited. Prior research highlights trust in AI and concerns about professional autonomy as key barriers to implementation. While explainability and system integration may foster trust, they may simultaneously threaten professional identity and decision authority. At the same time, perceived usefulness has been identified as the central driver of technology acceptance, although it is shaped by autonomyrelated concerns, particularly among physicians. This study integrates two experimental investigations (1,2) to examine how AI-CDSS design features jointly influence trust, autonomy-related perceptions, and acceptance across patients and physicians. Methods: The analysis combines and compares findings from two vignette-based experimental studies. The first study (n = 292) employs a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design manipulating AI explainability, workflow integration, and accountability to assess their effects on trust and professional identity threat among physicians. The second study consists of three experiments across patients (n = 209), potential future users (n = 1062), and physicians (n = 185), manipulating AI-CDSS system type (hybrid vs. autonomous) and recommendation risk (lifestyle vs. medical) (2 x 2 factorial design). Regression-based mediation and sequential mediation models (SPSS PROCESS Macro) were applied using bootstrapping procedures. Results: Results from the first study show that explainability and workflow integration significantly increase trust in AI-CDSS. At the same time, explainability and system-induced accountability increase perceived professional identity threat. Trust is negatively associated with identity threat and partially mediates the relationship between explainability and identity threat, indicating that trust can mitigate but not fully offset these concerns. Results from the second study demonstrate that perceived usefulness is the strongest predictor of intention to use among both patients, potential future users, and physicians. However, the underlying mechanisms differ. Patients and potential future users evaluate AI-CDSS primarily based on perceived usefulness, whereas physicians’ evaluations depend on professional autonomy preservation. For physicians, hybrid systems increase intention to use only indirectly through reduced professional autonomy concerns and increased perceived usefulness. High-risk medical recommendations consistently increase perceived or anticipated professional autonomy concerns across all groups but do not directly reduce perceived usefulness or intention to use. Conclusion: AI-CDSS acceptance is shaped by the interplay of trust, perceived usefulness, and professional autonomy-related concerns. Design features exhibit ambivalent effects, simultaneously enabling and constraining adoption. Successful implementation requires aligning system design with professional expectations, particularly by preserving physician decision authority while demonstrating clear clinical value.

items.title: Detecting and Mitigating Bias in AI Systems: A Methodological Approach to Social Inequality
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in decisions that affect health, employment, housing, justice, and social policy. Rather than neutral tools, they reflect the data on which they are trained, the objectives they optimize, and the contexts in which they operate, reinforcing and amplifying existing social inequalities. This paper addresses two interrelated questions: how can we detect bias across the AI lifecycle, and what technical and governance strategies can effectively mitigate it? Drawing on critical social science perspectives, empirical case studies from healthcare, housing, policing, and labor markets, and recent advances in fair machine learning (including causal debiasing, synthetic data generation, and fair representation learning), the paper develops a conceptual framework, grounded in sociological theories, spanning data collection, preprocessing, model training, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring. As an original contribution, the paper proposes two complementary analytical frameworks: a Social Harm-Intervention Mapping that recasts mitigation strategies in terms of the types of inequality they address, and an Accountability Matrix that maps agency and accountability gaps across social actors and pipeline stages. The paper argues that these frameworks provide social researchers and policymakers with more actionable guidance than conventional pipeline taxonomies because they foreground the social and institutional dimensions of AI-induced inequality rather than treating bias as a purely technical problem.

items.title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE EDUCATIONAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USE CONCERNS SCALE
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has brought pedagogical opportunities to the fore, but it has also made students’ affective responses, particularly concern related to AI usage, more visible. The aim of this study is to develop the Educational Artificial Intelligence Use Concerns Scale within the framework of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and AI concern and anxiety literature. The scale development process was conducted using the classical test theory approach and included the following stages: item pool creation, content validity through expert opinion, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and reliability-validity analyses. Data were collected from higher education students enrolled at [name of university / universities] in [city, country] through an online survey distributed via [institutional e-mail / classroom announcements / learning management system / social media], and separate samples were used for EFA (n = 300) and CFA (n = 129). CFA results yielded a two-factor structure, explaining 57.99% of the total variance. CFA findings revealed that the twofactor structure showed acceptable/excellent fit (χ²/df=1.88; CFI=.98; TLI=.98; RMSEA=.08; SRMR=.01). The scale’s internal consistency was found to be high (total α = .90), and convergent validity was supported by AVE values. The results indicate that the scale is a valid and reliable tool for measuring concerns related to AI use in higher education contexts. The scale can contribute to studies explaining the acceptance and integration of AI in education, particularly when used in conjunction with TAM variables, by examining the role of affective determinants in technology acceptance processes.

items.title: Digital Dependency and Academic Identity Among Postgraduate Students in the Era of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become embedded in everyday university life, often faster than institutional guidance has developed. This qualitative hermeneutic phenomenological study examined how postgraduate students experienced the boundary between generative-AI assistance and digital dependency, and how these experiences related to academic identity. In-depth, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eleven postgraduate students (five males and six females) at a public university in Saudi Arabia, selected through maximum-variation purposive sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for verification. Analysis followed Van Manen’s holistic, selective, and detailed approaches to phenomenological reflection. Two themes captured the experience: negotiating the boundary of digital dependency, and academic identity between agency and dependence. Rather than locating dependency in frequency of use, participants located it in the recurring transfer of substantive ideation, judgment, and authorship to the tool. Verification and the ability to explain and defend the final work helped preserve epistemic agency, whereas time pressure sometimes shifted practice toward substitution. Within this sample, strategic use as a coach, critic, or organizer supported confidence and skill development; extensive delegation was associated in participants’ accounts with diminished ownership, guilt, and concealment-oriented assessment practices. The findings offer a provisional, sample-grounded account of digital dependency and suggest that perceived ambiguity in institutional expectations may make concealment more salient, without establishing a causal relationship.

items.title: Digital Transformation and the Future of Higher Education: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review
items.abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is fundamentally changing the higher education institutions (HEIs) around the globe. The COVID-19 pandemic has drastically increased using digitally enabled approaches for teaching, learning, research, and administration, driven by the convergence of technologies encompassing the industry 4.0. Despite the various existing reviews that tackle digital transformation separately, some, such as those on the technology adoption or strategic planning, or pedagogical innovation, have limited scope and do not offer an overall, multi-dimensional synthesis. This rather comprehensive umbrella review combines dimensions, technologies, strategic processes and actors related to the implementation of DT in HEIs, based on the systematic and multivocal literature reviews, analyses via PRISMA, and thematic synthesises of articles, published from 2015 to 2024, in Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Springer Link and ACM Digital Library databases. A total of 47 studies in the analytical corpus, two of which were anchor reviews and 43 were complementary primary studies, were identified in an initial pool of 312 records. The findings showed that most digital transformation projects (DTIs) in the education sector are concentrated on competitive education (24%) and that the dominant enabling technologies are analytics (23%), cloud computing (20%), and artificial intelligence (16%). Most of all, just one-quarter of HEIs can speak with any degree of fluency about a digital strategy and only 56% of DTIs are part of a broader institutional agenda. The review concludes that, based on the importance of those topics in the curriculum, student demand satisfaction (12%) and digital culture (9%) fall short of expected levels of investment. The results are derived from the existing reviews and primary studies and thus share the limitations of the primary literature reviewed. The results highlight the need for university leaders to create digital strategies that are integrated, invest in faculty development and digital culture, and embrace a transformative approach instead of a technology-only approach to the implementation of digital transformation.

items.title: Digital Transformation, AI, and Inclusive Education: Creating Equitable Learning Ecosystems
items.abstract: This article examines the complex interrelationship between digital transformation, artificial intelligence adoption, and inclusive education in creating more equitable learning environments. Through mixed-methods research combining systematic literature review, survey data from 412 educational practitioners, and 37 semi-structured interviews with diverse stakeholders, the study explores how these three forces collectively reshape educational access, engagement, and outcomes for diverse learners. Statistical analyses reveal significant correlations between implementation patterns and equity outcomes (r=0.57, p<.001), with institutional commitment to inclusion (β=0.42, p<.001) emerging as the strongest predictor in regression models. Findings identify five key implementation patterns that significantly influence equity outcomes, including intentional design approaches, comprehensive integration strategies, continuous evaluation practices, stakeholder participation models, and balanced innovation-support frameworks. The study identifies critical barriers to equitable implementation, including persistent digital divides, algorithmic biases, professional development gaps, and governance challenges. The research contributes an empirically grounded Education Equity Technology (EET) model conceptualizing the interaction zones where these domains converge, while providing evidence-based recommendations for educational leaders and policymakers. These findings have important theoretical implications for understanding sociotechnical systems in education and practical applications for creating more inclusive digital learning environments.

items.title: Do narcissistic personality traits and immature defense mechanisms hinder communication and cooperation in pilots?
items.abstract: This study examines the safety operation behaviors of pilots within the framework of communication and cooperation, compares how these behaviors are affected by narcissistic personality traits, and compares the results for the correct evaluation and management of immature ego defense mechanisms, which are thought to be a factor triggering this relationship. The data were collected from 150 pilot participants working at airlines in Turkey using a survey data collection tool. It was observed that the participants frequently used the defense mechanisms of rationalization, isolation, and acting out. This result shows that pilots continue to exhibit the same behavior by providing acceptable reasons rather than trying to eliminate negative situations by discussing them realistically. It was also observed that they tend to focus only on the objective aspects of events and avoid discussing the parts that negatively affect them psychologically. In addition, it was found that narcissistic personality traits negatively affect the communication and cooperation behaviors of pilots, and immature ego defense mechanisms are a precursor that strengthens the narcissistic personality. It is thought that examining narcissistic personality traits within the framework of immature ego defense mechanisms and managing these mechanisms effectively will contribute greatly to aviation psychology research to prevent risks related to the human factor, which airline companies and authorities view as an important risk within safety management systems.

items.title: Dyadic: A Scalable Platform for Research on Human–Human and Human–AI Conversation
items.abstract: Conversation is ubiquitous in social life, but the empirical study of this interactive process has been thwarted by tools that are insufficiently modular and unadaptive to researcher needs. To relieve many constraints in conversation research, in the current tutorial, I present an overview and walkthrough of a new tool, Dyadic ( https://www.chatdyadic.com ), a web-based platform for studying human–human and human–artificial intelligence (AI) conversations using text-based or voice-based chats. Dyadic is distinct from other platforms by offering studies with multiple modalities, AI suggestions (e.g., in human–human studies, AI can suggest responses to a participant), live monitoring (e.g., researchers can evaluate chats between communicators in real time), and survey deployment (e.g., Likert-type scales, feeling thermometers, and open-ended text boxes can be sent to humans for in situ evaluations of the interaction), among other consequential features. No coding is required to operate Dyadic directly, and integrations with existing survey and participant-recruitment platforms are offered.

items.title: Earned Standing, Not Fluent Appearance: An Anatomical Review of Generative AI as an Epistemic Technology and Its Consequences for the Ontology of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This review anatomises Baum, McCarthy and Hannigan's chapter on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as an epistemic technology. The chapter's central claim is that GenAI does not merely extend what organisations can know; it changes the conditions under which they can trust what they treat as true. Outputs lacking Toulminian warrant are miscategorised as warranted knowledge because fluency, confidence and coherence mimic the ordinary cues of epistemic standing. The risk is dyadic at the point of use and network-level once miscategorised claims travel, accumulate authority and reshape institutional memory. Using epistemic networks (epinets) and a GenAI-supported strategic-planning cycle, the authors map four work modes — authenticated, automated, augmented and autonomous — onto paired dyadic and network risks, and derive stage-specific stewardship levers. The review reconstructs this argument joint by joint, states its strengths and limits, and places it against twelve competing or adjacent models of organisational knowing. It then traces the ontological and epistemological verticals that the chapter opens, and asks what the argument does to the ontology of GenAI itself: neither a retrieving instrument nor a knowing agent, but a proposition engine whose standing must be earned inside an infrastructure. Review article. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853.

items.abstract: Augmented Education: Artificial Intelligence, Neuroscience, and New Frontiers of Human Learning explores the transformation of the contemporary educational paradigm resulting from the convergence of intelligent technologies, neuroscience, and pedagogy. The work defines "augmented education" as a human-centered approach aimed at amplifying the cognitive, creative, and self-regulatory capacities of students and educators, preventing indiscriminate automation and technological dependence. Across three chapters, it examines the evolution of digital ecosystems toward adaptive and immersive environments, brain function in digital settings (analyzing neuroplasticity, attention, executive functions, and neuroethics), and the establishment of new pedagogical frontiers focused on challenge-based learning, formative assessment, and digital humanism.

items.title: Educational leadership and teacher effectiveness: A systematic literature review of empirical studies from 2015 to 2025
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of global educational reforms, school leadership and teacher effectiveness are widely recognized as key drivers of educational quality. However, existing research remains mostly fragmented, with limited comparative analysis of leadership models and insufficient attention to how contextual factors moderate leadership effects. Guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, this systematic review synthesizes 26 empirical studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science between 2015 and 2025. It examines how school leadership influences teacher effectiveness, compares the effects of different leadership models, and analyses the role of contextual moderators. Findings show that leadership affects teacher effectiveness through both direct and indirect pathways, with teacher self-efficacy serving as a central mediator. Instructional leadership enhances performance directly through goal clarity, curriculum management, and instructional supervision, whereas transformational leadership works more indirectly by activating teachers’ intrinsic motivation. Servant, participative, and collaborative leadership also show positive effects in specific contexts. Leadership effectiveness is strongly shaped by multilevel contextual factors, such as individual teacher characteristics, school organizational environments, and external socioeconomic and policy conditions. The review offers several practical implications. School leaders should act as both “context architects” and “meaning-makers,” flexibly combining leadership strategies to support teaching and professional growth. Teachers should strengthen instructional expertise and participate actively in professional learning communities, while policymakers should provide differentiated support and institutional safeguards. Future research should expand qualitative and mixed-method designs and conduct more cross-national and cross-cultural comparisons to deepen understanding of leadership mechanisms and improve teacher effectiveness across diverse educational settings.

items.title: Educator Trust Calibration as Sociotechnical Practice: A Field Study of Generative AI Use in Indian Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) systems are increasingly used in higher education, yet educator trust in these systems is often treated as an individual attitude rather than as a situated sociotechnical practice. Drawing on a 14-week field study with 42 faculty members at a mid-tier Indian technical university, this paper examines how educators encountered GenAI failures, interpreted system reliability, and developed verification-oriented routines across teaching, assessment, and administrative work. The study combines diaries, prompt logs, interviews, observations, surveys, reflective workshops, and structured red-teaming exercises. We analyze trust calibration as an ongoing process shaped by surface fluency, institutional authority, disciplinary expertise, peer reflection, and the labor of verification. Our findings identify three mechanisms of initial over-reliance: surface fluency deference, authority projection, and confirmation-seeking use. Participants later encountered fabricated citations, unstable answers, and locally specific policy failures that disrupted their mental models of GenAI reliability. We identify four educator trust postures—High-Adoption Uncritical, Low-Adoption Skeptical, Selective Verifiers, and Reflective Collaborators—and synthesize these into the Educator-AI Trust Calibration (EATC) framework. We do not claim that red-teaming caused trust recalibration. Instead, red-teaming functioned as one structured site within a broader field process through which educators made AI failures visible, negotiated verification responsibilities, and reworked use practices. The paper contributes a process-oriented account of educator-AI trust calibration and introduces the local knowledge verification gap as a mechanism through which fluent but unreliable GenAI outputs become difficult to contest in underrepresented institutional and regional contexts.

items.title: Effects of Generative AI–Supported Virtual Reality Dental Skill Training on Learning Performance, Visual Behavior, and Cortical Activation Among Dental Students: Stratified Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The rapid advancement of AI, particularly generative AI (GenAI), is reshaping educational paradigms. However, its utility in preclinical digital medical skills education remains insufficiently explored. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to investigate whether GenAI‑assisted training yields superior performance relative to traditional instruction in virtual reality (VR)-supported preclinical dental skill education. METHODS: A total of 123 eligible students from a top‑tier Chinese university completed the trial. Participants were stratified by baseline theoretical scores and randomly assigned within each stratum into two arms: the GenAI-assisted group (n=62) received ChatGPT guidance without human tutoring, with research assistants monitoring AI outputs solely for safety and error checking; the teacher-led control group (n=61) received on-site instructor guidance. Both groups underwent standardized VR-based dental skill training for 7 days. Assessments included dental operative skill examinations, functional near-infrared spectroscopy recording, continuous eye-tracking monitoring, visual-spatial ability tests, and questionnaires measuring self-regulated learning, learning emotions, and engagement. RESULTS: =3.88, Cohen d=0.70; P<.001). For secondary outcomes, the GenAI‑assisted group also demonstrated significantly lower cognitive‑load indicators (mean 0.180, SD 0.136) than the control group (mean 0.346, SD 0.150; P<.001), accompanied by more efficient visual attention allocation patterns and stronger activation in prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, visual association cortex, and temporoparietal junction brain regions. The GenAI‑assisted group showed better performance across low (P=.003), medium (P=.004), and high (P=.004) level visual-spatial ability tests. Among low-achieving participants, the largest between-group difference in self-regulated learning was found in favor of the GenAI-assisted group (P=.02). Better scores were also observed for the GenAI‑assisted group in learning enjoyment, as well as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. CONCLUSIONS: Students randomized to GenAI-assisted training had higher immediate operative scores than students receiving teacher-led instruction. Secondary cognitive, behavioral, and neurophysiological findings were exploratory and pointed toward a link between GenAI exposure and variations in skill‑acquisition metrics among dental students receiving VR-based training. The results offer preliminary insights regarding the potential integration of GenAI into preclinical dental skill education. items.title: Efficiency vs. safety in AI-enabled medical education: an ethical analysis of AI as a bridge or a wedge
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing medical education, promising faster workflows and richer learning resources while quietly reshaping how future clinicians think and act. This paper examines the central tension between efficiency and safety in AI-enabled medical education, asking when AI functions as a bridge that strengthens training and when it becomes a wedge that undermines it. Drawing on a targeted review of 1,266 pieces of literature on clinical decision support, diagnostic algorithms, and generative AI, we identify three interlocking ethical tensions: clinical efficiency versus health equity, cognitive convenience versus clinical judgment, and data-driven personalization versus professional integrity. Using role conflict theory, we demonstrate how these tensions manifest in the daily work of learners and clinical educators, who must simultaneously prioritize patient safety, promote independent reasoning, and adapt to AI-mediated workflows. We argue that medical education should treat AI not only as a technical tool but as a curricular and ethical problem: learners must be trained to question, calibrate, and sometimes refuse AI outputs. Framed this way, the task is not to decide for or against AI, but to design conditions under which it reliably acts as a bridge rather than a wedge.

items.title: Emotionally intelligent preference optimization for conversational behavior change support
items.abstract: Abstract Procrastination negatively affects productivity and well-being, yet current large language models (LLMs) often lack the nuanced emotional understanding necessary for effective behavior-change support. This study proposes emotionally intelligent preference optimization (EIPO), a unified framework integrating emotional chain-of-thought reasoning, teacher-guided self-correction, and direct preference optimization to enhance emotional intelligence in conversational user interfaces. Through ablation experiments evaluated using the emotional generation score (EGS), we demonstrate that EIPO significantly improves empathetic and constructive responses in procrastination-related interactions. Crucially, cross-model validation on Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-2-2B confirms EIPO’s model-agnostic design, with consistent EGS gains ( $$\Delta = +0.13$$ to $$+0.27$$ ) and robust independent evaluation using Claude-3.5-Sonnet. These findings establish EIPO as a principled, transferable framework for embedding emotionally intelligent behavior-change support into diverse LLM-driven CUIs.

items.title: Employee Experience Capital and Organizational Performance: An Integrated Framework for Understanding Workplace Resource Systems in Digitally Transformed Organizations
items.abstract: Contemporary organizations face the complex challenge of integrating diverse workplace resources—spanning digital tools, inclusive practices, sustainability initiatives, and well-being programs—into coherent systems that simultaneously support employee flourishing and organizational effectiveness. This theoretical paper develops the concept of Employee Experience Capital (EEC), defined as the integrated configuration of organizational resources that shape employees' holistic work experiences and generate sustainable competitive advantage. Drawing on Job Demands–Resources theory and the Resource-Based View of the firm, this paper identifies seven illustrative dimensions of EEC—digital autonomy, psychological safety climate, sustainability alignment, human–AI collaboration, restorative work design, learning climate, and well-being support systems—and provides systematic theoretical justification for their selection based on Self-Determination Theory's basic psychological needs framework. The paper proposes that EEC influences organizational performance through two empirically distinguishable mediating pathways: work meaningfulness (a cognitive-evaluative pathway) and experienced vitality (an affective-energetic pathway). Specific propositions predict which EEC dimensions more strongly affect each pathway. The framework advances theory by demonstrating how ostensibly disparate organizational practices function as an integrated resource system with emergent properties. The paper acknowledges boundary conditions, engages with competing theoretical perspectives, and discusses potential tensions and dark sides of EEC dimensions. Implications for research methodology and organizational practice are discussed.

items.title: Enterprise AI Security Architecture
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is becoming a core enterprise capability across customer service, software engineering, finance, supply chain, analytics, knowledge management, cybersecurity, and autonomous operations. However, the rapid adoption of Generative AI, Large Language Models, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, AI copilots, and agentic AI introduces a new attack surface that extends beyond conventional application security. Enterprises must protect models, prompts, embeddings, vector stores, APIs, tools, identities, business data, AI agents, orchestration layers, and cloud platforms while maintaining privacy, compliance, explainability, availability, and business trust. This paper proposes an Enterprise AI Security Architecture that integrates Zero Trust, Identity and Access Management, DevSecOps, model security, data security, prompt protection, API security, agent governance, threat detection, secure AI operations, incident response, and Responsible AI into a unified enterprise architecture. The framework establishes security controls across the complete AI lifecycle, including design, data preparation, model onboarding, RAG, agent execution, deployment, monitoring, and retirement. The proposed architecture enables organizations to scale enterprise AI securely across hybrid and multi-cloud environments while reducing cyber risk, protecting sensitive information, supporting regulatory compliance, and strengthening operational resilience.

items.title: Entrenamiento de fuerza gamificado en Secundaria: una adaptación del programa RETRAGAM
items.abstract: Low levels of physical activity during adolescence, together with the persistent underutilization of strength training within school settings, have prompted the development of interventions aimed at enhancing students’ motivation and engagement. The present study adapted the RETRAGAM protocol, a gamified functional strength-training program, for students enrolled in the first and second years of compulsory secondary education. The primary objective was to compare levels of amotivation and enjoyment between a group receiving a gamified strength-training intervention and a group participating in a traditional strength-training program. A total of 78 students (40 girls and 38 boys), aged 12–14 years, from a secondary school participated in the study. The intervention lasted 8 weeks and consisted of two weekly circuit-training sessions. Gamification was implemented through a Genially-based application featuring a superhero-themed narrative. Motivation was assessed using the Situational Motivation Scale, and enjoyment was measured using the Physical Activity Enjoyment Scale (PACES); both instruments were administered at the end of the intervention. The results revealed no statistically significant differences between the gamified and traditional strength-training groups in overall enjoyment (p_FDR = .657), intrinsic motivation (p_FDR = .601), or identified regulation (p_FDR = .601). However, a significant grade-level effect was observed for external regulation [F(1,74) = 5.60; p = .021; ηp² = .070], with higher scores among second-year students. In conclusion, although no significant differences were observed between conditions, gamification could be a promising pedagogical strategy for strength training in a school setting; therefore, further studies are needed to confirm its effectiveness.
